Ok let me preface this by saying ALL my hours on this game were after the 1.0 update. I only learned of this game history after I was 300h in.

If you are interested in learning it, I'd recommend watching the video by a youtuber called "The Good Trash", but if you want a quick recap, here it is:
The game was radically diferent before release. It was far more sandbox-driven, the story didn't really have a grasp on gameplay, and there was a TON more content. We're talking several cut bosses, biomes and entire features like the randomly generated monsters were a lot more developped. Unfortunately, the game had no developpement throughline. If a dev thought of a feature, it was gonna be added regardless of how well it would fits. 
Speaking of the devs, they were abused. Most basically came out of university and were hired as intern. This meant that they were paid little to none for their effort. Any that said anything were berated by the higher-ups, or straight up quit. This meant that most of the game's code was a buggy, unoptimized mess of spaghetti coding.
The 1.0 update tried to remedy this by essentially butchering the game into what it is now, which angered the community even more than it was already by the way the devs were treated.

Now, for my actual review.
The game's arstyle is gorgeous, the music (even if it gets repetive quickly) is top notch. 
Gameplay wise,  mining and general exploration feels great. 
Building is perhaps the best, there's so many diferent furnitures, blocks and decorations you can choose from for your base.
Fighting however... hoo boy. It is HORRIBLE. You can choose between ranged, melee and (later on) magic weaponry. You can craft some in each class, but if you want a worthwile weapon, you'll have to use one that is RANDOMLY GENERATED. Sure, there's unique weapons that alwasys have fixed stat (based on the planet you're on), but they are very rare and most aren't even worth it.
You're honestly better off using nothing but fast firing guns with some knockback, like a shotgun or something. Most dangerous enemies you'll be fighting are either flying, fast-moving, or just ranged guy that constantly run away.
Boss fights aren't much better either. The game WILL force you to fight these guys if you want to progress the story, and aside from like, the bird one, most devolve into a mess, be it by constantly spawning minions, having bad hitboxes (the 2nd to last final boss specifically), or because they have attacks that they do off-screen even if fully zoomed out.

Now, progression and story wise. This game's progression works in tiers. Every planet has a tier, going from 1 to 8. Higher tiered planets appear around specific stars, meaning you'll have use your spaceship to get over there. However, the big bad of the game broke your ship (and destroyed Earth but that's irelevant), so you'll have to at least take part in the story until the first boss to get the chance to progress.
After that? The story basically doesn't matter. Seriously you can just play the game without caring for it. Which is honestly a blessing in disguise, since it always the same formula of "Please go scan specific objects from these guys" to "Go defeat these guys' boss please". Repeat for every race except the umans and the Space cowboys.
It is so disappointing. Each race has a trope-infused but well crafted lore to it, so having all their quest being just fetch quest feels lazy.

And finally, we're gonna talk about performance. It is inconsistent at best, and its the game's messy code fault. Seriously this game is not optimized well. It can crash itself at complete random. Its rare but still. There's also a general problem with characters going to fast. If you fall from a great height, there's a chance the game will have trouble loading the terrain arround you. There's also time were the game just won't load a chunk at all. Or others were it lags as if you were having latency issues. In a single player game. Offline.
Oh and one final thing. The lower your FPS are, THE WORSE THOSE ISUES GET. No joke, if you limit your FPS to be under 60, these issues will pop up a ton more. It's not tied to your computer's performance, its the game itself tying a lot of the code to how high your FPS are.

I just can't recommend this game. I love this game but it is the definition of "wasted potential". If you're still interested in buying it, I can only recommend you mod it to hell and back
You'll see a lot of people using a mod called Frackin' universe. It's essetnially its own game, and is about as omnipresent as the Calamity mod is in the Terraria community. 
I personally don't recommend it, since it changes so much about the game that there's mods to mod a mod. Personnal recommendations are the Shellguard expansion, the Starforge, Anom's Outpost overhaul and Project Redemption.

Firstly, lets talk about the game. Starbound is a 2D extraterrestrial sandbox adventure game developed by Chucklefish.
Take on the role of a character who’s just fled their home planet, only to crash-land on another. You’ll embark on a quest to survive, discover, explore and fight your way across an infinite universe.

[b] Lets Discuss The Positives Now [/b]

[olist]
    [*] Huge universe to explore basically a 2D no mans sky(this one is actually a game).
    [*] Tons of crafting recipes,blocks and weapons.
    [*] Simple Controls easy to pick up and get used to.
    [*] Story Mission and quests to keep you entertained on your journey through space,
    [*] Creative and well designed boss battles which are abit challenging but that adds to the fun.
    [*] Gameplay even after main story mission.
    [*] Amazing community who are kind and helpful.
    [*] Character customization is brilliant and gives a wide variety of cosmetics to the player base.
    [*] Moddable- which is always a good thing it kills boredem after you have completed the game.
    [*] Simple Combat System- Keep in mind this is not a fighting game it is meant to be an exploration game.
    [*] Multiplayer- Over 20 people can join your server.
    [*] Design- Everything is well colored and presented its pure eyecandy.
    [*] Music- Very Calm And Soothing!
[/olist]

[b] Negatives now [/b]

I wasn't able to find huge flaws in the game but did come across some things i find annoying. Usually it was by chance but they were never frequent enough to ruin my gameplay. Every game has its cons StarBound is on the lighter side.

[olist]
    [*] Quests get repeatative and boring.
    [*]  Very hard to fight boss battles without friends, It requires alot of progress and items to solo one.
    [*] Minor Bugs- Sometimes the planet has invisible walls and theres nothing beyond them.

    [*] Glitches are a thing in this game and its annoying.

[h1] My Conclusion [/h1]

I say that StarBound is a fun time with friends. Theres alot of stuff to do its never boring. I also feel the need to address that StarBound is not a Terraria in space. I have played them both. I won't lie. I thought this game was going to suck.
I read most of the bad reviews saying that "Chucklefish has bad management" and "This is just another terraria clone."
But you know what?
It doesn't.
After reading most of the bad reviews, I had already removed the game from my wishlist. Until a friend of mine said I needed to get this game, me being the open-world loving exploration enthusiast that I am. So I said, and I quote, "Yeah, whatever mate."
And I got it. And I played it. And oh god did I love it. 
When I play a video game, I try not to get caught up in the developer drama. There are a plethora of stories on this game page about how Chucklefish "missed their chance" at increasing their popularity, and how the hype "waned out and died." I like to look past all of that. Same with Arkham Knight, the shitty PC port that it was. I played it, I liked it, and I didn't have to get caught up in all of that developer drama. And it's the exact same with Starbound.
If you look past the early access hell this game is going through, it's a really good game. It's fun to play around in, build in, and generally explore.
And it would be telling a lie if I said that the whole few hundred billion or however many unique variations of planets there are fact didn't impress me.
- Great music, although often repeats.
- Tons of biomes on different planets to explore.
- A surprisingly rich backstory, although the only way you could find this backstory is from randomly dropped codexes :(
- Randomly generated temples, tombs, castles, villages, research facilities among others are always a blast to explore.
- Surprisingly challenging for an open world platformer. (EDIT: That is, if you choose the normal mode.)
- There is no story. Litterally. You're planet explodes, your ship is broken, you fix it, and do quests for people around an interstellar outpost. (Not a very impressive one, I might add.) (And I also imagine that Chucklefish will be expanding on the story as they go, if Starbound ever makes it out of EA.)
- Randomly generated guns and swords are fun to collect. (also, the cosmetic armors are super awesome once you collect a full set.)
- Easter eggs. Everywhere.
In conclusion, you should get Starbound if you like exploring cool looking planets, collecting unique and fun to use items, and overall having fun killing unique monsters, looting enemy bases (and maybe a few friendly ones along the way), screwing around and decking out your space ship (Also, did I mention the ships? There are eight tiers to a ship, and once you get to your eighth tier, it's a blast decorating it.).
If you play games for story, dialogue, immersion and sidequests with a lot of effort put into it, this isn't the game for you.
You can listen to the bad reviews if you want, but what I'm trying to say is that it's not as bad a game as they say it is, for the reasons listed above.
But overall, it's a great game, and I do recommend it.
And it's not even finished yet!

Which one is better, Terraria or Starbound..? It's hard to say as both play out very different from one another. Where Terraria's main focus is on combat, Starbound is mostly about exploring and building. So just because you liked the former, doesn't mean you like the latter and vice versa. In the end it comes down to your personal preference and what you expect from them.

So what sets Starbound aside and makes it unique.. For starters it offers a huge galaxy with thousands of planets. Each one with its own different themes and the possibility of a wide variety of cities and dungeons. This can be everything from underwater metropolises to small farming villages, ruins of forgotten civilizations, creepy dungeons and hightec research labs. Even beneth a planets surface there's strange settlements and secrets to uncover as well.

These places will be populated with different races and animals. There are seven playable main races who all got their own lore and backstories. This is mostly presented in the form of different codices you can gather and read (some of which are pretty hilarious). Besides that there are numerous sub-races and factions running their own agenda. Some peaceful, others not so much. It's even possible to have some of them move in and offer unique supplies or serve as guards. 

This combined with some beautifully hand crafted metroidvania like missions where you undertake puzzles, dodge traps and fight bosses helps make Starbound a really interesting world to explore. All in all its a very colourful and diverse univers.

Starbound also allows for very different playstyles and almost everything is optional in order to progress. You can build villages or huge farms for profit, explore for resources or mine them, become self sufficient or survive by trade, do quests and gather a crew or roll as a lone wolf.. All valid options in order to survive. This also means your expected to find your own path and as such, there's very limited handholding. Which might throw some people off as there won't be a clear indicator on what to do next besides the overall objective. It's sorta like a "create your own adventure" story wherein the missions only serve as stretch goals.

Now combat ain't as streamlined as in most games of this genre. It's more a part of a whole, rather than the main focus. Building, farming crops, questing and exploring is as much a part of Starbound as combat is. So if your looking for a hack'n'slash combat focused experience, then you'll be disappointed and proberly find the game lacking as it can seem a little simplistic.

Don't get me wrong, combat in Starbound ain't bad. It's just different. For example there's no ammunition to speak of, instead every weapon draws from a commen energy pool. Also most weapons come with a special attack and the ability to dual wield them in almost any way you see fit. There's a wide variety of awesome and crazy weapons to help make it interesting like swords, spears, hammers, pistols, shotguns, sniper rifles, 'nade launches, flamethrowes, rocket launchers etc etc..

Starbound is a game suited for people that like to build, explore and create their own little adventures. If you take the time to enjoy its univers and all the different concepts it has to offer, then you'll get a plesant and enjoyable experience.

Closing argument and metaphor..
If Terraria is like a lego technic set, where you have to follow a specific schematic in order to achieve your goal. Then Starbound is a huge box of lego blocks that requires your imagination to reach it instead. It really only comes down to what you prefer.

I've loved this game for a LONG time but the developers gave up on it SO hard. So many good ideas that were never expanded on. The main quest is so tedious and boring, it takes all the fun our of exploration.

After 6-ish years of not playing, I decided to give Starbound a revisit as part of a personal "research" project. I even took notes and everything. My goal was to reflect on the games that made me want to make games, and Starbound was the first on my list.

Almost all of my notes were complaints.

The first conclusion I came to is that Chucklefish doesn't know how to make their players' time feel rewarding. An example that every Starbound player will know is that there's TOO. MANY. CONTAINERS. If you haven't played, that'll sound counterintuitive. (like a lot of things in this game tbh) Aren't boxes full of free stuff normally a GOOD thing? The crates in Starbound are full of useless items. Normally that would mean you could just ignore them, but from time to time they also contain items that are critical for progression, like weapons and manipulator modules. Loot isn't separated from junk, so you'll constantly be digging through a million crates hoping to get something useful.

Crafting progression is like any other game, you mine ore to progress yourself through "tiers", with each different metal only spawning on planets with specific biomes. As planets grow more dangerous, they require higher and higher tier protection, crafted using materials from the previous tier. It's perfectly straightforward and is one of the few mechanics in this game that makes sense. But the biomes progress linearly. It's essentially impossible to skip a tier, and every time you move on to the next level, your ass is going back down in the mines again. You end up doing this 6 times at minimum.

Everything feels the same, wherever you go. Starbound relies HEAVILY on RNG, and it's RNG that's not even that good. Once you've seen every biome, you've seen every planet. There's no meaningful difference between them. Its randomly generated weapons work the same way. The only real difference between weapons within the same class are damage type and secondary attack.

Planets are the same.
Weapons are the same.
Special abilities are the same.

The postgame suffers from yet another problem, and that's that it's an endless grind. Defeating the final boss unlocks dungeons called "Ancient Vaults", that you can grind repeatedly. The main reward from doing so are weapon enhancements (that only upgrade the damage) and terraformers you can use to change the biome of a planet. It requires at least two runs of the dungeon to craft each terraformer, and multiple more to run it. Each run of the dungeon requires you to buy a key with end-game materials. So in all likelihood you're gonna end up back in the mines a few more times.

Aside from not feeling rewarding, a lot of things in this game weren't thought through or just don't make sense. There are space stations called "Weapon trading stations". They don't sell usable weapons. You can tame wild creatures as combat pets. They still take contact damage, and primarily attack with melee, so they just end up charging in and immediately dying. And they remain dead until you get a late-game crafting station to revive them. Your environmental resistance is controlled by a backpack slot item called an EPP, and you lose all protection when it's unequipped. In previous updates, it was an "implant" that didn't take up inventory space. There are items still in the game that are completely vestigial. For example, there's a backpack slot item that provides light. It immediately becomes useless once you craft your EPP. There's no reason to take the EPP off, and it can be upgraded to provide light anyway.

The sandbox is completely neutered and decentivised via not giving the player any real motivation to set up a base in a planet and gift-wrapping them a shuttle that acts as a home from the getgo. Why build an elaborate base on a planet when you can do everything you would ever want to on your spaceship?

'Action' is not what I would describe the type of game Starbound is as. The combat is the videogame equivalent of throwing small pebbles at grass. Weapons lack satisfaction, taking damage from enemies doesn't feel significant, there is absolutely no recognisable progression equipment wise and anything you do get is handicapped with the lame energy system that the developers should've abandoned in early access. Imagine if every single weapon in Terraria required mana to use, was also as fun to use as the harpoon gun and if every enemy was only ever as fun to fight as a green slime. Starbound manages to make something that is half as fun as that.

The story is the most cookie-cutter nothingness I have ever seen in my entire life. The tutorial is the most tutorial tutorial I have ever played and it is a true accomplishment that, when you beat it, you are left to discover that the rest of the game is somehow worse. I couldn't recall a single bit of the main storyline because as far as I'm able to remember all that happens is that an old woman asks you to scan a bunch of objectives and then you a fight a boss. Rinse and repeat and then enjoy the expectation you're supposed to care about whatever happens next.

Why would I ever set up a base on a planet when there is nothing to be built on a planet that wouldn't be more convenient to build on my spaceship? Why would I ever invest in making tools when they break and I can just upgrade my matter manipulator? Why would I ever play Starbound?

I've grown to be so let down by this game because everything it promised is so far removed from what the game actually is. Coupled with the whispers of several workers being unpaid, no part of me could recommend this game earnestly or in jest.

This concept deserved so much better and so did my £13 I spent to play it.

[h1][b] TLDR: A vast but ultimately shallow vanilla experience that grows stale fast, with the modding community's deep additions doing most of the heavy lifting to make it worth recommending.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Steam Workshop integration
➕Extensive modding community
➕Infinite planets/game world size

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖No UI scaling option
➖No more content updates after 2019 (?)
➖Gameplay loop can get repetitive
➖Planets can be boring and too similar as you explore
➖Requires mods to add fun game systems - Vanilla can feel boring and often unfinished at times

I spent about 50 hours in this game initially, then spent my remaining time checking out the mods. There are some excellent mods on the Workshop that will really add some replay value, namely Frackin’ Universe and RPG Growth. 

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world is vast, but often meaningless. You do have infinite planets to explore, but beyond the different biomes, they don’t have much going on. Once you explore a few planets completely, you’ve seen all there is. 

The narrative isn’t anything special and revolves around you building up your spaceship and flying to different planets. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay loop consists of exploration and gathering, mixed with survival. It’s very similar to Terraria, with No Man’s Sky mixed in. You gather materials, and craft better gear, like Terraria, and then you explore a massive number of (mostly empty) planets over and over, like NMS. 
What really boosts the gameplay value here are the mods. They add a lot of depth to an otherwise decent experience. I would probably rate vanilla a 6. 

I’d say the game is normal difficulty. The combat seems less intricate than Terraria, but some of the survival aspects can make the game harder. In the beginning, it can be tough to get your food up and going, for example. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
A small step up from Terraria’s graphics. I’d say this is around PS2-era fidelity. Pretty simple. 

Runs fine, 60 FPS. I noticed no issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [8/10] [/b] [/h1]
Very good. I loved the planet side music. Probably the one area it triumphs over Terraria in. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
It has the replay diversity of an ocean, with the depth of a puddle, without mods. That is to say that the gameplay loop will grow stale quickly as you explore the same things over and over, but mods add a ton of new things. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
Starbound is a bit of an odd game. I found myself getting bored with it much quicker than Terraria, as the gameplay loop gets stale quickly after you discover some of the furthest long materials. However, what really added some much-needed systems to the game was mods. 

The vanilla experience leaves a lot to be desired as it can feel unfinished at times. The gameplay loop can get repetitive, and it simply lacks engaging systems or meaningful progression that has depth. Once you explore some planets and get resources….there just doesn’t seem to be much worth doing. Mods greatly change that. 

Both Frackin’ Universe and RPG Growth add some much-needed systems for the player to engage in. Things like an entire research tree with multiple forms of currency and tons of races with their own racial stats and abilities, and RPG classes like a Knight or Ninja, is what these mods add, respectively. And while these mods are wonderful and add in needed content, it’s slightly worrisome to me to recommend the game when the mods seem to be carrying it. I believe a game should be able to stand on its own, but I do also want players to experience the great things mod devs have done. 

If I had to rate the Starbound Vanilla experience, I would probably put it at a 5, classifying it as average. It has some good aspects, but other games, like Terraria, outclass it. 
Due to the needed mechanics that mods add, I would rate it a 6. As such, I would still recommend if you play it to spend some time in the vanilla game, but when you start getting bored, consider that the tutorial finished and try out some mods. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
I’d say full price of $15 is still a good deal considering the amount of content available, but due to its age, lack of “Completeness”, and overdependence on mods, I’d suggest getting it on sale.

There was a lot I liked and a fair number of things that I disliked in this game, so I'll start of with the gripes first

Gripes
- The story is utterly generic and completely forgetable *
- suffers from the minecraft issue even into the main release. (you will have the FAQ open at all times because the tutorial quests are bare bones at best and not at all indicitive of progression, but some people may like that in a masochistic way)
- It has a lot of stuff in it, and that is not always a good thing. There are things that while are cool to have are almost pointless, like incorporating a glorified MIDI reader for musical instruments. It feels very scatterbrained and without an identity, but it gives many options on how to progress and make a fortune in pixels, be it vagabonding, living pixel to pixel, mining out asteroids in mechs, or simply farming crops and shipping it off-world or selling your produce in local markets.
--- This gripe is more speaking as a person who hopped on in early access(angry koala) and more a gripe with the devs rather than the current state of the game. Pre full release, it did feel kind of empty with a nonexsistent quest or story, and I kind of would have liked it like that. it was way more friendly in terms of role play. The difficulty was a literal dice roll, where my literal first teleport down to a planet was in a micro dungeon with robots that shot lasers, on a planet that had acid rain and frequent meteor showers. This was challenging but not in an unfun way. Of course Chucklefish took steps to make it less russian roulette Dark Souls, but I feel that it also removed some of the can-get-curb-stomped-at-any-moment charm that was with older versions. All in all, the newer versions gave some sort of over arching goal, even if it sucked and was kind of unneeded or could be fleshed out.*
---The next gripe really only applies to lore junkies like myself. The story before had a degree of moral ambiguity, with totalitarian governments for everyone of every stripe, from theocracies to military juntas. Come post early access, the starship trooper/alien s mashup that was USCM was replaced by the so-sweet-and-utopian-that-it-would-give-you-a-toothache Terrene Protectorate, which looking from the outside for an intergalactic peacekeeping group  had very little influence unless you landed somewhere in the space booneys at the beginning of the game. The devs also removed all of the references of alcohol for some unexplained reason. It took off a lot of the edge and charm that I liked in the earlier versions.

Likes
-while the main quest is very generic and cookie cutter, you can do gear progression and role play without even noticing the main quest.*
-The building is very indepth and with many different materials and furniture. You can build so many different things, from Aztec style pyramids to futuristic cities. 
-after you plow through the main story, the game opens up into a randomly generated dungeon style system, which extends the game's already huge playtime.
-There will almost be something to do, due to the sheer amount of stuff in the game.
-modding in steam workshop and outside of it is huge
-good to play solo and to play with friends, with steam multiplayer and traditional IPs being used.

All in all, I do recommend the full release of Starbound, but I probably won't buy any other Early Access title from Chucklefish ever again, due to their initial mismanagement.

I've had never been a huge Minecraft fan and I've never played Terraria....like ever.  So I bought this game based entirely on the fact that, "everyone else is doing it so it must be good."  I know, dad always said just because everyone else is jumping off a cliff doesn't mean I have to do it too....... But sometimes it's fun to jump off the cliff with everyone else.  With that known, this review will be from a non-Minecraft/Terraria fan and what my impressions are.

My first game play into Starbound was solo.  After all, I didn't want to look like a complete n00b when I start playing with friends.  I think I was expecting some sort of 2D Minecraft, to which I wasn't let down in that aspect.  There was mining, crafting, building your home/base all those things that make Minecraft interesting.  Then I see one of those cute little aliens and I'm like, "oh cool, hopefully it won't attack me at a snail’s pace like the monsters in Minecraft.........ohh, oohh.. WTF it's spraying some sort of fire barf all over me and jumping at me.  Good gods get it off... I'm dead."  It would take me another few fights similar to that to get the hang of the combat system which thankfully is much more active than Minecrafts.  Being one who likes challenging game play, (my favorite game series is Monster Hunter after all,) this was the first thing in Starbound that made me want to play more.  Hanging out more in the game, discovering that different mobs do have different attacks and there are boss monsters, I've not been let down in this area.  

After reading a bit online about how to get a good start, (if you’re a game player that likes to be lead by the nose to everything you need to do in a game then you may not enjoy this game as much...) I felt I was ready for multi-player.  A friend of mine asked if I'd like to join him and off we went.  After playing a bit I've seen that multiplayer is certainly where it’s at in this game.  Don’t' get me wrong, solo was fun but there's just something about teaming up and traveling to other planets, building fancy bases, exploring random dungeons, it's all much more fun when you've got a friend to hang out with.  Throw in some Skype so you can hear each other panic as some monster from hell rips though your group and your set for some very fun times.

Overall I enjoy the game a lot.  Even in early access there's a ton of content and things to do and well worth the money spent to buy it.  I eagerly look forward to what the future holds for this game.

Pros:  
Minecraft style gathering, building, and crafting
Hundreds of sandbox worlds in one game
Challenging monster and boss fights
Tons of content in terms of places to explore, an entire universe full of planets
Each planet has a different feel to it
Survival feels like survival since you actually have to eat and watch that you don't get too cold
Multiplayer is tons of fun
Replay value is super high
Great music
Should only get better with age

Cons:
Very little guidance.  You will need out of game resources to figure out the game entirely
Some monster fights can feel repetitive as they have similar combat modes
Planets can start to feel similar in terms of graphics
Different races seem to be only cosmetically different at the moment
2D pixel graphics may turn some off
Still in beta/early access so there are some crashes, glitches (tee hee) and maximization things that happen

Please note that many of the cons are things that will/may go away or be changed as the game leaves beta and gets more fleshed out.  Overall though the game is already well worth the listed price of $14.99us and if it's a game style you think you'd enjoy it will be money well spent.

9/10

Starbound is a procedurally generated universe where you can plunder endless amounts of dungeons, build colonies, and mod the shit out of it. It's a cute indie with co-operative multiplayer which makes up for its unassuming appearance with the sheer amount of content the developer provides, supports and continues to shell out.

Both the pixel art and soundtrack are both easy on your senses, creating an immersive atmosphere and inspiring ambience for late night galactic voyages. Especially fun if you have some friends who want to build a settlement or tag along for an adventure. Prepare for a time-sink.

This could have been something truly special. I remember the first versions were so charm and love filled, albeit at the expense of unpaid underage labor, but beyond that the game has fallen so flat that I can't logically find a single reason why you would pick this over Terraria.
